bib.author: Hecke, M. van
bib.abstract: Amorphous materials as diverse as foams, emulsions, colloidal suspensions and granular media can jam into a rigid, disordered state where they withstand finite shear stresses before yielding. Here we review the current understanding of the transition to jamming and the nature of the jammed state for disordered packings of particles that act through repulsive contact interactions and are at zero temperature and zero shear stress. We first discuss the breakdown of affine assumptions that underlies the rich mechanics near jamming. We then extensively discuss jamming of frictionless soft spheres. At the jamming point, these systems are marginally stable (isostatic) in the sense of constraint counting, and many geometric and mechanical properties scale with distance to this jamming point. Finally, we discuss current explorations of jamming of frictional and non-spherical (ellipsoidal) particles. Both friction and asphericity tune the contact number at jamming away from the isostatic limit, but in opposite directions. This allows one to disentangle the distance to jamming and the distance to isostaticity. The picture that emerges is that most quantities are governed by the contact number and scale with the distance to isostaticity, while the contact number itself scales with the distance to jamming.
bib.title: Jamming of soft particles: geometry, mechanics, scaling and isostaticity

bib.abstract: We describe experiments on a two-dimensional granular Couette system consisting of photoelastic disks undergoing slow shearing. The disks rest on a smooth surface and are confined between an inner wheel and an outer ring. Only shearing from the inner wheel is considered here. We obtain velocity, particle rotation rate (spin), and density distributions for the system by tracking positions and orientations of individual particles. At a characteristic packing fraction, γc≃0.77, the wheel just engages the particles. In a narrow range of γ, 0.77{\textless}{\textasciitilde}γ{\textless}{\textasciitilde}0.80 the system changes from just able to shear to densely packed. The transition at γc has a number of hallmarks of a critical transition, including critical slowing down, and an order parameter. For instance, the mean stress grows from 0 as γ increases above γc, and hence plays the role of an order parameter. Also, the mean particle velocity vanishes at the transition point, implying slowing down at γc. Above γc, the mean azimuthal velocity decreases roughly exponentially with distance from the inner shearing wheel, and the local packing fraction shows roughly comparable exponential decay from a highly dilated region next to the wheel to a denser but frozen packing further away. Approximate but not perfect shear rate invariance occurs; variations from perfect rate invariance appear to be related to small long-time rearrangements of the disks. The characteristic width of the induced “shear band” near the wheel varies most rapidly with distance from the wheel for γ≃γc, and is relatively insensitive to the packing fraction for the larger γ’s studied here. The mean particle spin oscillates near the wheel, and falls rapidly to zero away from the shearing surface. The distributions for the tangential velocity and particle spins are wide and show a complex shape, particularly for the disk layer nearest to the shearing surface. The two-variable distribution function for tangential velocity and spin reveals a separation of the kinematics into a slipping state and a nonslipping state consisting of a combination of rolling and translation.
bib.title: Kinematics of a two-dimensional granular {Couette} experiment at the transition to shearing

bib.abstract: This contribution considers the critical time increment (Δtcrit) to achieve stable simulations using particulate discrete element method (DEM) codes that adopt a Verlet-type time integration scheme. The Δtcrit is determined by considering the maximum vibration frequency of the system. Based on a series of parametric studies, Δtcrit is shown to depend on the particle mass (m), the maximum contact stiffness (Kmax), and the maximum particle coordination number (CN,max). Empirical expressions relating Δtcrit to m, Kmax, and CN,max are presented; while strictly only valid within the range of simulation scenarios considered here, these can inform DEM analysts selecting appropriate Δtcrit values.
bib.title: Empirical assessment of the critical time increment in explicit particulate discrete element method simulations

bib.author: Pol, Antonio and Artoni, Riccardo and Richard, Patrick and Conceição, Paulo Ricardo Nunes da and Gabrieli, Fabio
bib.abstract: The kinematics and the shear-induced alignment of elongated particles in confined, heterogeneous flow conditions are investigated experimentally. Experiments are conducted in an annular shear cell with a rotating bottom wall and a top wall permitting confinement of the flow. Flow kinematics and particle orientation statistics are computed by particle tracking using optical imaging. Translational velocity profiles show an exponential decay, and surprisingly, only the slip velocity at the bottom is influenced by the particle shape. Rotations are highly frustrated by particle shape, more elongated particles showing, on average, a lower angular velocity. In addition, a clear shear-rate dependency of the proneness of a particle to rotate is observed, with a stronger inhibition in low shear zones. The average orientation of the particles does not correspond to the main flow direction, they are slightly tilted downwards. The corresponding angle decreases with the particles’ elongation. Orientational order was observed to increase with particles’ elongation, and surprisingly was not affected by the applied confinement. A weak but systematic decrease of the orientational order was observed in regions of higher shear rate. At the particle-scale, angular velocity fluctuations show a strong correlation with local particle orientation, particles being strongly misaligned with the preferential particles’ orientation rotating faster. This correlation becomes stronger for more elongated particles, while is almost unaffected by the applied confinement.
bib.title: Kinematics and shear-induced alignment in confined granular flows of elongated particles

bib.keywords: Rheology, alignment, dimensional analysis, non spherical particles
bib.author: Campbell, Charles S.
bib.abstract: Granular flow rheology can be divided into two global regimes: the elastic, which is dominated by force chains, and the inertial, which is nearly free of force chains. As the propensity of a material to form force chains should be strongly influenced by particle shape, this paper is an attempt to assess the effects of shape on flow regime transitions through computer simulations of shear flow of ellipsoidal particles. On one hand, the results show that at a given concentration, ellipsoidal particles generate smaller quasistatic stress than spheres, likely a result of their ability to form denser packings. But at the same time, large aspect ratio ellipsoids more readily form force chains and demonstrate elastic behavior at smaller concentrations than spheres. This is shown to be due to a tradeoff between a shear-induced particle alignment that tends to minimize the interference of the particles and the shear flow, and the particle surface friction, which works to rotate the particles into the flow.
bib.title: Elastic granular flows of ellipsoidal particles

bib.author: Nagy, Dániel B. and Claudin, Philippe and Börzsönyi, Tamás and Somfai, Ellák
bib.abstract: We study the rheology of dense granular flows for frictionless spherocylinders by means of 3D numerical simulations. As in the case of spherical particles, the effective friction μ is an increasing function of the inertial number I, and we systematically investigate the dependence of μ on the particle aspect ratio Q, as well as that of the normal stress differences, the volume fraction, and the coordination number. We show in particular that the quasistatic friction coefficient is nonmonotonic with Q: from the spherical case Q=1, it first sharply increases, reaches a maximum around Q≃1.05, and then gently decreases until Q=3, passing its initial value at Q≃2. We provide a microscopic interpretation for this unexpected behavior through the analysis of the distribution of dissipative contacts around the particles: as compared to spheres, slightly elongated grains enhance contacts in their central cylindrical band, whereas at larger aspect ratios particles tend to align and dissipate by preferential contacts at their hemispherical caps.
bib.title: Rheology of dense granular flows for elongated particles

bib.author: Cai, Ruihuan and Xiao, Hongyi and Christov, Ivan C. and Zhao, Yongzhi
bib.abstract: The diffusion of nonspherical particles has not been well understood due to the complexity of their contact mechanics and self-organization of their orientations. We perform discrete element method simulations of monodisperse ellipsoids in a shear flow with Lees-Edwards boundary conditions to quantify the relation between the diffusion coefficient and the flow parameters. The results indicate that the particle aspect ratio strongly affects the diffusion coefficient by influencing the particle orientation and alignment. We develop a scaling law for the diffusion coefficient perpendicular to the flow direction, Dyy, which combines the influences of the shear rate , the solids fraction f, the effective particle diameter deff and the particle aspect ratio Z. We show that , where kd is a dimensionless pre-factor, and a fit is obtained for the functional form of χ(f, Z). This scaling law will be useful in developing continuum transport models for applications.
bib.title: Diffusion of ellipsoidal granular particles in shear flow

bib.keywords: Rheology, Suspensions, To\_read\_again, dimensional analysis, mu-I
bib.author: DeGiuli, E. and Düring, G. and Lerner, E. and Wyart, M.
bib.abstract: Rheological properties of dense flows of hard particles are singular as one approaches the jamming threshold where flow ceases both for aerial granular flows dominated by inertia and for over-damped suspensions. Concomitantly, the length scale characterizing velocity correlations appears to diverge at jamming. Here we introduce a theoretical framework that proposes a tentative, but potentially complete, scaling description of stationary flows. Our analysis, which focuses on frictionless particles, applies both to suspensions and inertial flows of hard particles. We compare our predictions with the empirical literature, as well as with novel numerical data. Overall, we find a very good agreement between theory and observations, except for frictional inertial flows whose scaling properties clearly differ from frictionless systems. For overdamped flows, more observations are needed to decide if friction is a relevant perturbation. Our analysis makes several new predictions on microscopic dynamical quantities that should be accessible experimentally.
bib.title: Unified theory of inertial granular flows and non-{Brownian} suspensions

bib.keywords: Algorithm, DEM simulation, Numerical method, non spherical particles
bib.author: Podlozhnyuk, Alexander and Pirker, Stefan and Kloss, Christoph
bib.abstract: Particle shape representation is a fundamental problem in the Discrete Element Method (DEM). Spherical particles with well known contact force models remain popular in DEM due to their relative simplicity in terms of ease of implementation and low computational cost. However, in real applications particles are mostly non-spherical, and more sophisticated particle shape models, like superquadric shape, must be introduced in DEM. The superquadric shape can be considered as an extension of spherical or ellipsoidal particles and can be used for modeling of spheres, ellipsoids, cylinder-like and box(dice)-like particles just varying five shape parameters. In this study we present an efficient C++ implementation of superquadric particles within the open-source and parallel DEM package LIGGGHTS. To reduce computational time several ideas are employed. In the particle–particle contact detection routine we use the minimum bounding spheres and the oriented bounding boxes to reduce the number of potential contact pairs. For the particle–wall contact an accurate analytical solution was found. We present all necessary mathematics for the contact detection and contact force calculation. The superquadric DEM code implementation was verified on test cases such as angle of repose and hopper/silo discharge. The simulation results are in good agreement with experimental data and are presented in this paper. We show adequacy of the superquadric shape model and robustness of the implemented superquadric DEM code.
bib.title: Efficient implementation of superquadric particles in {Discrete} {Element} {Method} within an open-source framework

bib.note: Publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
bib.author: Brito, Carolina and Ikeda, Harukuni and Urbani, Pierfrancesco and Wyart, Matthieu and Zamponi, Francesco
bib.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
bib.abstract: Amorphous packings of nonspherical particles such as ellipsoids and spherocylinders are known to be hypostatic: The number of mechanical contacts between particles is smaller than the number of degrees of freedom, thus violating Maxwell’s mechanical stability criterion. In this work, we propose a general theory of hypostatic amorphous packings and the associated jamming transition. First, we show that many systems fall into a same universality class. As an example, we explicitly map ellipsoids into a system of “breathing” particles. We show by using a marginal stability argument that in both cases jammed packings are hypostatic and that the critical exponents related to the contact number and the vibrational density of states are the same. Furthermore, we introduce a generalized perceptron model which can be solved analytically by the replica method. The analytical solution predicts critical exponents in the same hypostatic jamming universality class. Our analysis further reveals that the force and gap distributions of hypostatic jamming do not show power-law behavior, in marked contrast to the isostatic jamming of spherical particles. Finally, we confirm our theoretical predictions by numerical simulations.
bib.title: Universality of jamming of nonspherical particles

bib.keywords: Algorithm, Contact detection, DEM simulation, Numerical method
bib.author: Descantes, Yannick and Tricoire, Fabien and Richard, Patrick
bib.abstract: The present paper sheds new light on ongoing drawbacks of three classical algorithms dedicated to initial contact detection between overlapping convex polyhedra, (i) Cundall’s common plane, (ii) Nezami’s fast common plane and (iii) Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi’s algorithm (GJK). Solutions to these drawbacks are suggested and implemented into revised versions of those three algorithms, which are further benchmarked for accuracy and speed using nine overlapping contact situations. The benchmarking results show that the revised version of GJK, called GJK-TD, and Nezami (revised) return values of the contact normal components and overlap depth which are identical to machine precision, whereas Cundall (revised) results differ beyond the ninth decimal place. Furthermore, for a given contact situation, GJK-TD returns those values within a few tens of microseconds on average, whereas Nezami (revised) and Cundall (revised) are respectively 6 and 65 times more computationally intense. It is believed that the robustness and efficiency of GJK-TD will boost its use into DEM simulations, all the more that this versatile algorithm may easily be customized to detect contact between convex polyhedra and spheroid particles.
bib.shorttitle: Classical contact detection algorithms for {3D} {DEM} simulations

bib.author: Nagy, Dániel B and Claudin, Philippe and Börzsönyi, Tamás and Somfai, Ellák
bib.abstract: The rheology of a 3-dimensional granular system consisting of frictional elongated particles was investigated by means of discrete element model calculations. A homogenous shear ﬂow of frictional spherocyliders was simulated, and a number of rheological quantities were calculated. In the framework of the μ(I) rheology, the effective friction was found to be a non-monotonic function of the aspect ratio for interparticle friction coefﬁcient μp 0.4, while it was an increasing function for larger μp. We reveal the microscopic origin of this peculiar non-monotonic behaviour. We show the non-trivial dependence of the velocity ﬂuctuations on the dissipation regime, and trace back the behaviour of the normal stress differences to particle-level quantities.
bib.title: Flow and rheology of frictional elongated grains

bib.keywords: Perspectives, Soft matter, Squishy granular matter, To\_read
bib.author: Barés, Jonathan and Cárdenas-Barrantes, Manuel and Cantor, David and Renouf, Mathieu and Azéma, Émilien
bib.abstract: Softer than soft, squishy granular matter is composed of grains capable of significantly changing their shape (typically a deformation larger than 10\%) without tearing or breaking. Because of the difficulty to test these materials experimentally and numerically, such a family of discrete systems remains largely ignored in the granular matter physics field despite being commonly found in nature and industry. Either from a numerical, experimental, or analytical point of view, the study of highly deformable granular matter involves several challenges covering, for instance: (i) the need to include a large diversity of grain rheology, (ii) the need to consider large material deformations, and (iii) analysis of the effects of large body distortion on the global scale. In this article, we propose a thorough definition of these squishy granular systems and we summarize the upcoming challenges in their study.

title: Topological groups from matrices of sets
summary:
We give a general construction of topological groups from combinatorial
structures such as trees, towers, gaps, and subadditive functions. We connect
topological properties of corresponding groups with combinatorial properties of
these objects. For example, the group built from an $\omega_1$-tree is
Frech\'{e}t iff the tree is Aronszajn. We also determine cofinal types of some
of these groups under certain set theoretic assumptions.

title: Multimodal Framework for Explainable Autonomous Driving: Integrating Video, Sensor, and Textual Data for Enhanced Decision-Making and Transparency
summary:
Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are poised to redefine transportation by enhancing
road safety, minimizing human error, and optimizing traffic efficiency. The
success of AVs depends on their ability to interpret complex, dynamic
environments through diverse data sources, including video streams, sensor
measurements, and contextual textual information. However, seamlessly
integrating these multimodal inputs and ensuring transparency in AI-driven
decisions remain formidable challenges. This study introduces a novel
multimodal framework that synergistically combines video, sensor, and textual
data to predict driving actions while generating human-readable explanations,
fostering trust and regulatory compliance. By leveraging VideoMAE for
spatiotemporal video analysis, a custom sensor fusion module for real-time data
processing, and BERT for textual comprehension, our approach achieves robust
decision-making and interpretable outputs. Evaluated on the BDD-X (21113
samples) and nuScenes (1000 scenes) datasets, our model reduces training loss
from 5.7231 to 0.0187 over five epochs, attaining an action prediction accuracy
of 92.5% and a BLEU-4 score of 0.75 for explanation quality, outperforming
state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of each
modality, while qualitative analyses and human evaluations highlight the
model's ability to produce contextually rich, user-friendly explanations. These
advancements underscore the transformative potential of multimodal integration
and explainability in building safe, transparent, and trustworthy AV systems,
paving the way for broader societal adoption of autonomous driving
technologies.

title: scDataset: Scalable Data Loading for Deep Learning on Large-Scale Single-Cell Omics
summary:
Modern single-cell datasets now comprise hundreds of millions of cells,
presenting significant challenges for training deep learning models that
require shuffled, memory-efficient data loading. While the AnnData format is
the community standard for storing single-cell datasets, existing data loading
solutions for AnnData are often inadequate: some require loading all data into
memory, others convert to dense formats that increase storage demands, and many
are hampered by slow random disk access. We present scDataset, a PyTorch
IterableDataset that operates directly on one or more AnnData files without the
need for format conversion. The core innovation is a combination of block
sampling and batched fetching, which together balance randomness and I/O
efficiency. On the Tahoe 100M dataset, scDataset achieves up to a 48$\times$
speed-up over AnnLoader, a 27$\times$ speed-up over HuggingFace Datasets, and
an 18$\times$ speed-up over BioNeMo in single-core settings. These advances
democratize large-scale single-cell model training for the broader research
community.

title: Knowledge-guided Contextual Gene Set Analysis Using Large Language Models
summary:
Gene set analysis (GSA) is a foundational approach for interpreting genomic
data of diseases by linking genes to biological processes. However,
conventional GSA methods overlook clinical context of the analyses, often
generating long lists of enriched pathways with redundant, nonspecific, or
irrelevant results. Interpreting these requires extensive, ad-hoc manual
effort, reducing both reliability and reproducibility. To address this
limitation, we introduce cGSA, a novel AI-driven framework that enhances GSA by
incorporating context-aware pathway prioritization. cGSA integrates gene
cluster detection, enrichment analysis, and large language models to identify
pathways that are not only statistically significant but also biologically
meaningful. Benchmarking on 102 manually curated gene sets across 19 diseases
and ten disease-related biological mechanisms shows that cGSA outperforms
baseline methods by over 30%, with expert validation confirming its increased
precision and interpretability. Two independent case studies in melanoma and
breast cancer further demonstrate its potential to uncover context-specific
insights and support targeted hypothesis generation.

title: Ergodic behaviors in reversible 3-state cellular automata
summary:
Classical cellular automata represent a class of explicit discrete spacetime
lattice models in which complex large-scale phenomena emerge from simple
deterministic rules. With the goal to uncover different physically distinct
classes of ergodic behavior, we perform a systematic study of three-state
cellular automata (with a stable `vacuum' state and `particles' with $\pm$
charges). The classification is aided by the automata's different
transformation properties under discrete symmetries: charge conjugation,
spatial parity and time reversal. In particular, we propose a simple
classification that distinguishes between types and levels of ergodic behavior
in such system as quantified by the following observables: the mean return
time, the number of conserved quantities, and the scaling of correlation
functions. In each of the physically distinct classes, we present examples and
discuss some of their phenomenology. This includes chaotic or ergodic dynamics,
phase-space fragmentation, Ruelle-Pollicott resonances, existence of quasilocal
charges, and anomalous transport with a variety of dynamical exponents.

bib.abstract: We introduce a pair of time-reversible models defined on the discrete space–time lattice with three states per site, specifically, a vacancy and a particle of two flavours (species). The local update rules reproduce the rule 54 reversible cellular automaton when only a single species of particles is present, and satisfy the requirements of flavour exchange (C), space-reversal (P), and time-reversal (T) symmetries. We find closed-form expressions for three local conserved charges and provide an explicit matrix product form of the grand canonical Gibbs states, which are identical for both models. For one of the models this family of Gibbs states seems to be a complete characterisation of equilibrium (i.e. space and time translation invariant) states, while for the other model we empirically find a sequence of local conserved charges, one for each support size larger than 2, hinting to its algebraic integrability. Finally, we numerically investigate the behaviour of spatio-temporal correlation functions of charge densities, and test the hydrodynamic prediction for the model with exactly three local charges. Surprisingly, the numerically observed ‘sound velocity’ does not match the hydrodynamic value. The deviations are either significant, or they decay extremely slowly with the simulation time, which leaves us with an open question for the mechanism of such a glassy behaviour in a deterministic locally interacting system.

bib.abstract: The problem of characterizing the complexity of quantum dynamics—in particular of locally interacting chains of quantum particles—will be reviewed and discussed from several different perspectives: (i) stability of motion against external perturbations and decoherence, (ii) efficiency of quantum simulation in terms of classical computation and entanglement production in operator spaces, (iii) quantum transport, relaxation to equilibrium and quantum mixing, and (iv) computation of quantum dynamical entropies. Discussions of all these criteria will be confronted with the established criteria of integrability or quantum chaos, and sometimes quite surprising conclusions are found. Some conjectures and interesting open problems in ergodic theory of the quantum many problem are suggested.

bib.abstract: We discuss a simple deterministic lattice gas of locally interacting charged particles, for which we show coexistence of ballistic and diffusive transport. Both, the ballistic and the diffusive transport coefficients, specifically the Drude weight and the diffusion constant, respectively, are analytically computed for a particular set of generalized Gibbs states and may independently vanish for appropriate values of thermodynamic parameters. Moreover, our analysis, based on explicit construction of the matrix representation of time-automorphism in a suitable basis of the algebra of local observables, allows for an exact computation of the dynamic structure factor and closed form solution of the inhomogeneous quench problem.

bib.abstract: A dynamical Lie algebraic method for the construction of quantum invariants of motion in non-integrable many-body systems of infinite size is proposed and applied to a simple but generic toy model, namely an infinite kicked t - V chain of interacting spinless fermions. The transition from an  integrable via quasi-integrable ( intermediate) to a  quantum ergodic (quantum mixing) regime in parameter space is investigated. A  dynamical phase transition between an  ergodic and  intermediate (neither ergodic nor completely integrable) regime in thermodynamic limit is proposed. The existence or non-existence of local conservation laws corresponds to the intermediate or ergodic regime, respectively. The computation of time-correlation functions of typical observables by means of local conservation laws is found to be fully consistent with direct calculations on finite systems.

bib.abstract: We define a quantum Perron–Frobenius master operator over a suitable normed space of translationally invariant states adjoint to the quasi-local C* algebra of quantum lattice gasses (e.g. spin chains), whose spectrum determines the exponents of decay of time correlation functions. The theoretical ideas are applied to a generic example of kicked Ising spin 1/2 chains. We show that the ‘chaotic eigenmodes’ corresponding to leading eigenvalue resonances have fractal structure in the basis of local operators.

\author{ Agata Smoktunowicz}

\begin{abstract}

 This paper presents a method for constructing flat deformations of associative algebras. We will refer to this method as method two because it is a  generalisation of the method obtained in \cite{DDS}.  
 The deformations obtained using the first two methods are of  polynomial type. We also present a third method, for the construction of deformations from $N$  to $A$, for a semisimple algebra $A$.

  As an applied example,  we   answer a question posed by Michael Wemyss on deformations of Acons.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
  Recently, some deep and rich connections between noncommutative algebra and algebraic geometry have been found; for example, W. Donovan and M. Wemyss introduced {\em contraction algebras}--noncommutative algebras arising in connection with invariants of flops \cite{DW}, and G. Brown and M. Wemyss provided a purely algebraic description of these algebras by presenting explicit generators and defining relations \cite{GV, W2}.
  
 This paper is motivated by questions posed by Michael Wemyss concerning deformations of  contraction algebras; one type of these questions asks whether a given contraction algebra can be deformed to a concrete semisimple algebra found by geometric methods.
Such questions are motivated by links to Gopakumar-Vafa (GV) invariants and are formulated in a purely algebraic context.  
 We develop our third method for constructing deformations from an algebra $N$ to a semisimple algebra $A$ and as an application we answer a question posed by Michael Wemyss about deformations of the  contraction algebra of dimension $8$.  
In our forthcoming paper \cite{paper2}, we show that all flat deformations from an algebra $N$ into semisimple algebra $A$ can be  
 obtained using our third method (under some additional assumptions). In \cite{paper2} we  also give further applications for contractions algebras by answering some other  questions by Michael Wemyss.

For results related to geometric and algebraic  deformations of noncommutative algebras   which appear in this context,  see \cite{BD, HT, 10, Toda, K1, K2, W}. 

$ $

   
Our second method is for constructing flat deformations of associative algebras. This is a generalisation of our first method obtained in \cite{DDS}.  
 The second is obtained by removing  some assumptions from the first, thus making it possible for it to be applied in  more varied situations. One of the motivations for the second method comes from a question of Michael Wemyss on the geometric  meaning of deformations of contraction algebras to various types of algebras.  It is also possible to combine Methods $2$ and $3$ to construct deformations into a direct product of some compies of algebras $A_{1}, \ldots , A_{n}$.

 Deformations of noncommutative algebras appear in various contexts;
 for  example, in \cite{Iain}, I. Gordon  used symplectic reflection algebras to obtain deformations of some important classes of noncommutative algebras (related to group actions), and L. Vendramin recently used deformations of Hopf-algebras to answer longstanding open problem about Nichols algebras. 
 Deformations of quantum algebras are  used in quantum integrable systems, for example in  \cite{Doikou}.

 The deformation theory of associative algebras was initiated by Murray Gerstenhaber in
the 1960s. Gerstenhaber described
the rich connection of deformations of associative algebras and their Hochschild cohomology. Hochschild cohomology of noncommutative algebras is investigated intensively \cite{SWbook}.

 In mathematical physics, there are many applications of deformations of Lie algebras. 
Such deformations can  sometimes be obtained from deformations of noncommutative algebras (in research of  Axel Kleinschmidt and Joaquim Gomis).   Hochschild cohomology in associative deformations of a semiring  induces deformations of a Lie algebra expansion.
 Deformations of Lie (super) algebras appear in the classification of certain kinds of Lie algebras given in terms of a Lie subalgebra $h$ and a module $m$, which one may think of as deformations of some  abelian extensions \cite{jose1}. 
 Such deformations are also used to study geometries whose automorphisms are filtered deformations of graded Lie (super) algebras.   This is a part of an approach leading to the classification of supersymmetric supergravity backgrounds \cite{jose2}.
In these areas, it is often of interest to  classify all deformations of a given Lie algebra  (subject to some natural conditions).

  Deformations of commutative algebras is an important research area with scope  way beyond this paper   (although our second and third methods can be used to construct deformations of commutative algebras).
One motivation for investigating deformations is coming from physics (for example, Kontsevich's  paper on deformation quantization of Poisson manifolds).
  Another motivation  is moduli theory in algebraic geometry.
Deformations of modules over some classical commutative rings are one of tools in symplectic geometry. 

 
Our methods do not use Hochschild cohomology and derivations, and can be considered as a method of choice for constructing examples of algebraic deformations (see  \cite{3, SWbook} and \cite{Markl} for some other methods).  Notice that   new methods of deforming Hecke algebras and graded Hecke algebras have been described \cite{SW}.  Deformations of graded Hecke algebras may be used to describe Hecke algebras.

 All of the algebras and deformations we consider are associative and have an identity element. 
 

\section{Background information}

 We recall a definition of a flat deformation. An algebra $A$ can be flatly deformed to an algebra $B$ if
\begin{enumerate}

\item There is a formal deformation $A\{ t\}$ of $A$ such that $A\{t_{0}\}$ is isomorphic to $B$ for some $t_{0}\in \mathbb C$.  
 Notice that $A\{0\}$ is equal to $A$, since $A\{t\}$ is the formal deformation of $A$.

\item The dimension of $A\{c\}$ for $0\leq c \leq t_{0}$ is the same as the dimension of $A$.

\end{enumerate}


We recall the definition of the formal deformation of $A$ from \cite{SWbook}.
 
\begin{defn}\cite{SWbook} A formal deformation $(A_{t}, \circ, +)$ of a $\mathbb C$-algebra $(A, \cdot, +)$ is an associative $k$-bilinear multiplication $\circ $ on the $\mathbb C\{t\}$ module $A\{t\}$ (where $A\{t\}$ is the set of power series with coefficients from $A$.)

Recall that $A\{t\}$ has natural structure of $\mathbb C\{t\}$-module given by 
\[t^{j}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty }a_{i}t^{i}= \sum_{i=0}^{\infty }a_{i}t^{i+j}.\]
\end{defn}

 $(A_{t}, \circ, +)$ is a deformation of {\em polynomial type} of a $\mathbb C$-algebra $(A, \cdot, +)$ if for all $a,b\in A$, $a\circ b\in A[t]$, where $A[t]$ denotes the polynomial ring in variable $t$ and coefficients in $A$.


$ $


In this paper, we only consider the case when $A$ is a finitely dimensional $\mathbb C$ algebra. Moreover, we only consider  deformations $A\{t\}$ of $A$ in which the image of the identity element in $A$ acts as the identity element in $A\{t\}$. All algebras considered in this paper are associative, and usually noncommutative.

 Let $b_{1}, \ldots , b_{n}\in A$ be a base of $A$ as a linear vector space over field $\mathbb C$. Note that every element of $A\{t\}$ can be written in the form
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}f_{i}(t),\]
 for some $f_{i}\in \mathbb C\{t\}$.
 
Then, we have a well defined multiplication on $A\{t\}$ given by
\[(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}f_{i}(t))\circ (\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}f_{i}(t))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{i}\circ b_{j}f_{i}(t)f_{j}(t).\]

Notice that this multiplication is associative, since the multiplication $b_{i}\circ b_{j}$ is associative, so $(A\{t\}, \circ, +)$ is an associative algebra (as it is a subalgebra of the algebra of power series ring $A\{x\}$ with coefficients in $A$ and in indeterminate $t$). We assume that $(A, \circ , +)$  has an identity element $1_{A}$, so we can identify elements of $\mathbb C\{t\}$ with elements of $A$. In particular if $f(t)\in \mathbb C\{t\}$ then $f(t)1_{A}$ is not a zero divisor of $A\{t\}$.


 We will now recall some definitions from \cite{DDS}, as we will be using the same notation.

%\begin{defn}
   %  Let $S$ be a subset of a $k$-algebra $A$ for a commutative unital ring $k$. Then $S$ is a \textbf{generating set} if all elements of $A$ can be written as a $k$-linear sum of products of %elements of $S$ using the operations in $A$.
%\end{defn}


\begin{notation}
    We will denote by $\mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle$ the polynomial ring over $\mathbb C$ in two non-commuting variables, $x$ and $y$.
\end{notation}


\begin{notation}\label{not:monomials}
    Consider monomials of the ring $\mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle$. We can order the monomials using shortlex ordering by specification $x<y$ and setting $1$ as the least monomial. Note that this means that if a monomial $p_i\in \mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle$ is a product of $n_i$ elements from the set $\{x,y\}$, then $p_i<p_j$ whenever $n_i<n_j$. If $n_i=n_j$, then  we can let $p_i=a_1a_2...a_{n_i}$ and $p_j=b_1b_2...b_{n_j}$, where $a_m, b_m\in\{x,y\}$. Then $p_i<p_j$ if and only if $a_k<b_k$, where $k$ is the first index where $a_m$ and $b_m$ differ.  We denote the monomials of $\mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle$ by $ p_1,p_2\dots$
where $p_i<p_{j}$ for $i<j$. 
\end{notation}

\begin{notation}
    We will denote by $\mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle \{t\}$ the power series ring in variable $t$ with coefficients from $\mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle $. By $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle [t]$ we will  denote the polynomial ring in variable $t$ over the ring  $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle $.  By $\mathbb C\{t\}$ we denote the power series ring in variable $t$ and coefficients from $\mathbb C$. By ${\mathbb C}[t]$ we denote the polynomial ring in variable $t$. 
\end{notation}


\begin{notation}
   Let $R$ be a ring and $I$ be an ideal of $R$, then elements of the factor ring $R/I$ will be denoted as $r+I$, where $r\in R$.
 Notice that $r+I=s+I$ for $r,s\in R$ if and only if $r-s\in I$.
\end{notation}
\section{Part 1: Semisimple algebras}\label{part2}

 Flat deformations of noncommutative algebras to finitely semisimple algebras appear in  noncommutative resolutions of algebraic singularities research and is related to GV invariants.

In this section we modify the method from \cite{DDS} to obtain our third method for constructing flat deformations from an algebra $N$ to a semisimple algebra $A$.  In a following paper it will be shown that every flat deformation from $N$ to $A$, with $A$ semisimple,  is  
 obtained in this way (under some additional assumptions) \cite{paper2}.  
  Notice that the third method is not needed in its whole generality in \cite{paper2} as in \cite{paper2}  it can be assumed that  all $D_{i}$ are one dimensional, and all $u_{i}$ are $1$. The third method is introduced in whole generality so as to make the calculations of concrete deformations easier. 



$ $

 We first introduce some notation. 
 Recall that  ${\mathbb C}\langle x,y\rangle \{t\}$ is the power series ring in variable $t$  over the free algebra ${\mathbb C}\langle x,y\rangle$. Let $1$ denote the identity element of the algebra ${\mathbb C}\langle x,y\rangle \{t\}$.  By \[F={\mathbb C}\{t\}[t^{-1}]\] we denote the field of fractions of ${\mathbb C}\{t\}$. 

 
    Let $n, k', n_{1}, \ldots , n_{k}$ be natural numbers (larger than $0$). For each $i\leq k'$, we fix a polynomial  $g_{i}(x)\in {\mathbb C}[t](x)$ of degree $d_{i}$ ($g_{i}$ is a polynomial in variable $x$ and with coefficients in  ${\mathbb C}[t]$). We assume that the coefficient at the largest power of $x$ in $g_{i}(x)$ is $1$.  We also fix $u_{i}=x+I_{i}\in F[x]/I_{i}$ where $I_{i}$ is the ideal generated by $g_{i}(x)$ in the polynomial ring $F[x]$. We assume $u_{i}u_{j}=0$ for $i\neq j$.   Observe that $u_{i}$ is a root of $g_{i}(x)$ in $F[x]/I_{i}$.


 We assume  that each   $g_{i}(x)$ has no multiple roots (so polynomials $g_{i}(x)$ and $g_{i}(x)'$  have no common divisors), and is not divisible by $x$. We will also denote $g_{i}(x)=g_{i}(x)(t)$ since coefficients of $g_{i}(x)$ depend on $t$. 
By $g_{i,s}(x)$ we denote the polynomial $g_{i}(x)$ where 
 $t=s$, so $s$ was substituted at places of $t$ in the entries of $g_{i}(x)$.
 We denote $v_{i}=x+I_{i}'$ where $I_{i}'$ is the ideal generated by $g_{i,s}(x)$ in the polynomial ring ${\mathbb C}[x]$. We assume $v_{i}v_{j}=0$ for $i\neq j$.   Observe that $v_{i}$ is a root of $g_{i,s}(x)$ in $F[x]/I_{i}'$.

$ $

 We denote \[A'=\oplus _{i=1}^{k'}M_{n_{i}}({\mathbb C}\{t\}[u_{i}][t^{-1}]),\]
 where ${\mathbb C}\{t\}[u_{i}][t^{-1}]$ consists of  finite sums of elements from $ {\mathbb C}\{t\}u_{i}^{k}t^{-j}$ for $k=0,1,\ldots $, 
$j=1,2, \ldots $. Similarly, ${\mathbb C}[t][u_{i}][t^{-1}]$ consists of  finite sums of elements from $ {\mathbb C}u_{i}^{k}t^{j}$ for $k=0,1,\ldots $, 
$j\in \mathbb Z$.

\subsection {\bf Method $3$.}\label{333} 

 Let notation be as at the beginning of Section \ref{part2}.

Then: \begin{enumerate}
 \item  We define
 $f: {\mathbb C}\langle x,y\rangle \{t\} \rightarrow A'$ to be the homomorphism of ${\mathbb C}\{t\}$-algebras  given by : 
  \[      f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{k'}b_{i}(u_{i}, t) \] 
        \[f(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{k' }c_{i}(u_{i},t),\]
 for some $b_{i}(u_{i}, t), c_{i}(u_{i}, t)\in M_{n_{i}}({\mathbb C}[t][u_{i}][ t^{-1}])$. 

 Therefore, there are $\alpha _{i,j,l}, \beta _{i,j,l}\in \mathbb C$ and an integer $\iota $ (which may be  negative) such that 
  \[b_{i}(u_{i},t)=\sum_{j=\iota, \iota +1, \ldots , l=0, \ldots , d_{i}-1}\alpha _{i,j,l}u_{i}^{l}t^{j},\]
\[  c_{i}(u_{i},t)=\sum_{j=\iota, \iota +1, \ldots , l=0, \ldots , d_{i}-1}\beta _{i,j,l}u_{i}^{l}t^{j}.\]  
  We also have $f(1)=1_{A'}$, where $1_{A'}$ is the identity element of $A'$.
 
  
\item Denote \[{\bar A}=\oplus_{i=1}^{k'} M_{n_{i}}(E_{i})\] 
 where $\mathbb E_{i}=\oplus _{i=1}^{d_{i}}{\mathbb C}.$

\item  Suppose that there is a real number $s\neq 0$ such that
 $f(x)(s)=\sum_{i=0}^{m }b_{i}(v_{i}, s)$ and $f(y)(s)=\sum_{i=0}^{m }c_{i}(v_{i},s)$ generate $n$-dimensional  $\mathbb C$-algebra.  
 Where $b_{i}(v_{i}, s)$ and $\sum_{i=0}^{m }c_{i}(v_{i},s)$ are obtained from $b_{i}(u_{i}, t)$ and $\sum_{i=0}^{m }c_{i}(u_{i},t)$ by substituting $t=s$, $u_{i}=v_{i}$ where $v_{i}$ is defined at the beginning of section \ref{part2}. Notice that for sufficiently small $s>0$,  $g_{i,s}(x)$ has no multiple roots (see Lemma \ref{pierwiastki}). Also $v_{i}v_{j}=0$ for $i\neq j$. 
 We also assume that for every $e\in \mathbb R$, $e>0$ we can find such $s\in (0, e)$.
 

\item We also assume that there is a natural number $\gamma $ such that
 \[Im(f)\subseteq t^{-\gamma} \oplus_{i=1}^{k'}M_{n_{i}}({\mathbb C}[t][u_{i}]).\]
 Recall that ${\mathbb C}[t][u_{i}]$ consists of sums of elements from ${\mathbb C}t^{i}u_{i}^{j}$ for $t,j\geq 0$. 
\item We denote 
$I=ker(f)$ the kernel of $f$.

 \item We denote: 
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathcal{N} := {\mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle\{t\}}/I.
    \end{equation*}
  
 
  Now we evaluate $t$ at various values in $T = [0, \infty)$. We denote by $N_s$ the  algebra that arises from $\mathcal{N}$ by evaluating $t$ at $s$. We also denote $N$ for the algebra $N_{0}$.


 The algebra $\mathcal{N}$ and the family of algebras $\{N_t\}$ are the output of this method. 

\item By Theorem \ref{thm formal deformationnew} the family $\{N_t\}$ is a deformation of $N=N_{0}$ and by Theorem \ref{thm:iso1new}  it holds that $A \in \{N_t\}$.
 
Moreover, there is $0<\epsilon \in \mathbb R$, such that  algebra $N_{s}$ is isomorphic to ${\bar A}$ for all $s\in (0,\epsilon)$. Also the algebra $N=N_{0}$ has the same dimension as the algebra ${\bar A}$. 
 Therefore, this method produces a flat deformation from $N$ to $\bar A$ for $t\in [0, \epsilon]$. 
 \item By Theorem \ref{polynomial} this method produces also a deformation of polynomial type with the same properties as in the subpoint 7 above. 

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{ Method $3$ gives deformations from $N$ to $\bar A$.}\label{A}
%In this section we generalise results from Subsection \ref{123} to show that  Method $3$ produces deformations from $N$ to $\bar A$, as mentioned in subsection \ref{333}.
Denote,  \[{ A}=\oplus_{i=1}^{k'}M_{n_{i}}({\mathbb C}+{\mathbb C}u_{i}+\cdots +{\mathbb C}u_{i}^{d_{i}-1}),\] 
 where $u_{i}$ are as in Subsection \ref{333}. 
Recall that in Subsection \ref{333} we assumed that there is a natural number  $\gamma $ such that $Im(f)\subseteq t^{-\gamma}A[t]$. 

\begin{prop}\label{basisnew}  
    Let notation and assumptions be as in subsection \ref{333}. Then the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item  There exist elements 
$q_{1}, q_{2}, \dots , q_{n}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle [t]$ such that for every 
$r\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle \{t\}$ we have 
      \[  f(r)\in \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb C\{t\} f(q_{i}).\]
    Moreover $n=\dim {\bar A}.$ 
 Moreover, we can assume that $q_{1}=1$ and then $f(q_{1})=1_{\bar A}$. 
 
\item  There exists a natural number $m$ such that $rt^{m}\in im(f)$ for every $r\in {\bar A}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}  Let $A$ be as above. 
Then $A$ is a linear space over $\mathbb C$, of the same dimension as $\bar A$. 
%The lines $1-40$ are exactly the same as in the proof of Proposition \ref{basis} with the $A$ as defined $2$ lines above. 

  Let $k_1$ be the smallest possible integer such that for some integer $k_1$  that for some non-zero $e_{1}\in A$ we we have
\[e_{1}t^{k_1}+\sum_{i=k_{1}+1}^{\infty }\alpha_{i,1}\cdot t^{i} \in im (f)\]
for some $\alpha_{i,1}\in A$. Let $k_2$ be the smallest possible integer such that for some  $e_{2}\in A$, $e_{2}\notin \mathbb C \cdot e_{1}$ we have 
\[e_{2}t^{k_{2}}+\sum_{i=k_2+1}^{\infty }\alpha _{i,2} \cdot t^{i} \in im (f)\]
for some $\alpha_{i, 2}\in A$.

 Notice also that by the minimality of $k_{1}$ we have $k_{2}\geq k_{1}$.

Let $k_{3}$ be the smallest possible integer such that 
 for some $e_{3}\in A$, $e_{3}\notin \mathbb C \cdot e_{1}+C\cdot e_{2}$ we have 
\[e_{3}t^{k_{2}}+\sum_{i=k_3+1}^{\infty }\alpha _{i,3} \cdot t^{i} \in im (f)\]
for some $\alpha _{i,3}\in A$. Notice also that by the minimality of $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ we have $k_{3}\geq k_{2}$.

 Continuing in this way until we can add new elements $k_{i}, e_{i}$, we define 
 natural numbers $k_{1}\leq k_{2}\leq \ldots \leq k_{n'}\subseteq \mathbb N$
 and a set \[\{e_{1}, \ldots , e_{n'}\}\subseteq A.\] Observe that $A$ has dimension $n$ so $n'\leq n$.

{\em We claim that $n'=n$.}
Let $q_{1}, q_{2}, \cdots , q_{n'}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle \{t\}$ be such that 
\[f(q_{1})=e_{1}t^{k_1}+\sum_{i=k_{1}+1}^{\infty }\alpha_{i,1}\cdot t^{i}\]
\[f(q_{2})=e_{2}t^{k_2}+\sum_{i=k_{2}+1}^{\infty }\alpha_{i,2}\cdot t^{i}\]
 and so on. 

Let now $r\in \mathbb C\langle x, y\rangle ,$ then 
$f(r)=\sum_{i=-\gamma}^{\infty}a_{i}t^{i}$ for some $a_{i}\in A$.  
 By the leading pseudoterm of $f(r)$ we will mean $a_{k}t^{k}$ with $i$ minimal such that $a_{k}t^{k}\neq 0$. Observe that 
 by the minimality of $k_{1}$ we have $k\geq k_{1}$. k
 By the construction of elements $e_{1}t^{k_1}, e_{2}t^{k_2}, \ldots , e_{n'}t^{k_{n'}}$ we have 
 that the leading pseudoterm $a_{k}t^{k}$ of $f(r)$ satisfies 
\[a_{k}t^{k}=\sum _{i=1}^{m}\zeta _{i}(t)e_{i}t^{k_i}\] for some $\zeta _{i}(t)\in \mathbb C\{t\} $ (as otherwise we could add $a_{k}t^{k}$  as an element $e_{n'+1}t^{k_{n'+1}}$).


Now \[f(r)-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\zeta _{i}(t)f(q_{i})\] will have the leading pseudoterm with larger power of $t$. Denote $r'=r-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\zeta _{i}(t)f(q_{i})$.
  Next we can again repeat the analogous 
argument for $f(r')$  and again obtain the leading pseudoterm at even larger power of $t$.
 Because powers of leading pseudoterms will increase this will imply that 
\[f(r)= \sum_{i=1}^{m}\gamma _{i}(t)f(q_{i})\]
 for some $\gamma _{i}\in \mathbb C\{t\} $ (see Remark $1$ at the end of this proof for additional explanation why this holds). 
This shows that \[im (f)\subseteq \sum_{i=1}^{n'} \mathbb C\{t\} f(q_i).\]
 
$ $

We will now show that $n'=n$. Observe that $n'\leq n$ since $A$ has dimension $n$ as a vector space over $\mathbb C$. 
 If $n'<n$, we can find elements $e_{n'+1}, \ldots , e_{n}\in A$ such that $e_{1}, \ldots , e_{n}$ spans $A$ as $\mathbb C$-linear space.


 Recall that by Subsection \ref{333},  $f(x)= \sum_{i=0}^{k'}b_{i}(u_{i}, t) $,  $f(y)= \sum_{i=0}^{k' }c_{i}(u_{i},t)$. 
We know that at $t=s$ elements $f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{k'}b_{i}(v_{i}, t) $, $f(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{k' }c_{i}(u_{i},t)$ generate $n$-dimensional algebra  (we will denote this algebra as $A''$). 
Therefore there are elements $m_{2}, \ldots , m_{n}$ (each of them is a product of elements $x,y$) and  $m_{1}=1$
  such that $f(m_{1})(s), \ldots , f(m_{n})(s)$ span $A''$ as a vector space over $\mathbb C$.  

{\em Remark on notation.} Notice that  $f(m_{1})$ is a product of some elements $f(x), f(y)$ and hence they are polynomials in variable $t$, so we can write $f(m_{1})=f(m_{1})(t)$ and  
the element $f(m_{i})(s)$ denotes element $f(m_{i})(t)$ where we substitute $t=s$).  


 By the definition of the function  $f$, it follows that 
 there is a $n$ by $n$ matrix  $M=M(t)$ with entries from $t^{-\gamma }{\mathbb C}[t]$ and such that $u(t)=v(t)M(t)$. We can write $M=M(t)$ since entries of $M$ depend on $t$.

 We can now consider a homomorphism $\sigma: A[t, t^{-1}]\rightarrow A''$ of $\mathbb C$ algebras given by $\sigma (t)=s$, $\sigma(t^{-1})=s^{-1}$, $ \sigma(u_{i})=v_{i}$, where $v_{i}$ are as in subsection \ref{333}, so $v_{i}v_{j}=0$ for $i\neq j$ (it can be verified that it is a well defined homomorphism by representing $u_{i}$ as matrices).
Note that that we can apply $\sigma $ to the each entry of $M=M(t)$ and we denote 
$\sigma (M)=M(s),$ similarly $u(s)=(f(m_{1})(s), \ldots , f(m_{n})(s))$.
Observe  that by applying $\sigma $ to the equation
 $u(t)=M(t)v$ we obtain   
\[u(s)=\sigma (v)M(s).\] 
  
 Observe that columns of $M(s)$ cannot be linearly dependent over $\mathbb C$ since elements \[f(m_{1})(s), \ldots , f(m_{n})(s)\] are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$ (since we assumed that they span $\bar A$).


 Therefore $M(s)$ is a non-singular matrix (so its determinant is non zero).   Therefore $M(t)$ is a  matrix whose determinant is nonzero (as if determinant of $M(t)$ was zero then specialised at $t=s$ it would also be $0$).

 Consequently, by using the Cramer's formula (considering $M$ as matrix whose entries are from the field of fractions of ${\mathbb C}[t]$) we get
\[det(M(t))v=u(t)M'(t),\] where $M'(t)$ is $n$ by $n$ matrix obtained by Cramer's rule from $M(t)$ (so $M'(t)$ has entries  entries from $t^{-\gamma \cdot n}{\mathbb C}[t]$). Note that $u_{i}u_{i}=0$ for $i\neq j$. As usual, $det (M(t))$ denotes the determinant of $M(t)$. 


 Therefore $e_{i}\cdot det(M(t))t^{\gamma \cdot n}\in \sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb C}[t]f(m_{i})(t)$. Therefore,  $det(M(t))\in t^{k}(1+h(t)){\mathbb C}$ for some $h(t)\in t{\mathbb C}[t]$ and some $k$. 
 Consequently  $e_{i}(t^{m'}(1+h(t))\in Im(f)$ for sufficiently large $m'$ and for some $h(t)\in t{\mathbb C}[t]$. 
 This implies that $e_{i}t^{m'}$ is the leading pseudoterm of an element from $Im(f)$. 
This implies that $n=n'$.
 Observe also that $e_{i}t^{m'}\in (1+h(t))^{-1}Im(f)\subseteq Im(f)$ and $(1+h(t))^{-1}\in \mathbb C \{t\}$.  
 Therefore, for sufficiently large $m'$ and  for  every $a\in A$  
 \[at^{m'}\in Im(f).\] Consequently 
$at^{m'+j}\in t^{j}Im(f)$, hence for any $g(x)\in A\{t\}$ we have 
$t^{m'}g(x)\in Im(f)$.

 We will now show that we can assume that $q_{i}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle [t] $, so that they are polynomials in variable $t$.

 Let $q_{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty } d_{i}t^{i}$ for some $d_{i}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle $.   
Let $m>max(k_{1}, \ldots , k_{m})$. 
 Denote $q'=\sum_{i=0}^{m+\gamma  }d_{i}t^{i}$ for some $\gamma >0$.
 Then  $f(q_{i}')$ and $f(q_{i})$  have the same leading pseudoterms for each $i$ (since leading pseudoterms appear near $t^{k_{i}}$ and $k_{i}<m$).
 We can therefore use the same reasoning from the first part of this proof  for $q_{i}'$ instead of $q_{i}$ (at each step choosing $q_{i}'$ instead of $q_{i}$) and we obtain that   
 $Im(f)\subseteq \mathbb C\{t\}f(q_{1}')+\cdots +\mathbb C\{t\}f(q_{1}')$.  Therefore we can take elements $q_{1}', \ldots , q_{n}'$ instead of 
 $q_{1}', \ldots , q_{n}'$. So we can assume that $q_{1}, \ldots , q_{n}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle [t]$. 


\end{proof}



\begin{prop}\label{basesnew}
Let notation and assumptions be as in subsection \ref{333}.   Recall that we denoted $ker(f)=I$. 
 Then the following holds:

\begin{enumerate}
\item   Suppose $\sum_{i=1} ^n \beta _{i}q_{i}\in I$ for some $\beta _{i}\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$. Then $f(\sum_{i} ^n \beta _{i}q_{i})=0$ and consequently  $\beta _{i}=0$ for every $i\in\{1,2,\dots, n\}$.

 \item Moreover, all elements of $I$ are $\mathbb C \{t\}$-linear combinations
 of elements 
\[p_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k}q_{i}+t\xi_{i,k}(t)q_{i})\]
for some $k\in \mathbb N, \zeta _{i,k}\in \mathbb C$, $\xi _{i,k}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$ where  $p_{k}\in {\mathbb C}\langle x,y\rangle$ are as in Notation \ref{not:monomials}. 
\end{enumerate}
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i q_i \in I$. Recall that $I= \ker f$, so
\[0 = f(\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i q_i) = \sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i f(q_i). \]
 Let notation be as in the proof of Proposition \ref{basisnew}, then 
\[f(q_m) = e_{m}t^{k_m}+\sum_{i=k_{m}+1}^{\infty }\alpha_{i,m}e_i\]
for each $m\in \mathbb N$. Now suppose that not all $\beta_i$ equal $0$. 
 Let $\xi_{i}t^{j_{i}}$ be the leading term of $\beta _{i}$, for these  $\beta _{i}$ which are non-zero.
We know that \[0= f(\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i q_i). \]
 On the other hand the leading pseudoterm of the power series$ f(\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i q_i)$ is a sum of some of the elements $\xi_{i}t^{j_i}e_{i}t^{k_{i}}$ and therefore is non-zero since $e_{1},\ldots ,e_{n}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$ (by their construction).

 %Let $\beta _{m}\in  \zeta _{m}t^{l_{m}}+t^{l_{m}+1}\mathbb C \{t\}$ for some natural number $l_{m}$ and some $
%\zeta _{m}\in \mathbb C$. 
% Therefore, the leading pseudoterm of $\sum_{i=1}^{m'}\beta_i f(q_i)$ is a sum of some  number of elements %$e_{m}\zeta_{m}t^{k_{m}+l_{m}}$
% so it cannot be zero, unless $\beta _{i}=0$. This concludes the proof.

Therefore, all $\xi _{i}=0$, so $\beta _{i}=0$. 


$ $


We will now show that all elements of $I$ are $\mathbb C\{t\}$-linear combinations
 of elements 
\[p_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k}q_{i}+t\xi_{i,k}(t)q_{i})\]
for some $k\in \mathbb N, \zeta _{i,k}\in \mathbb C$, $\xi _{i,k}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$ (recall that $p_{k}$ are monomials from $\mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle $).
 Proof is similar as in \cite{DDS}, but we use polynomials instead of power series.

 Because $Im(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb C\{t\}f(q_{i}) $ then there are 
$\zeta _{i,k}\in \mathbb C$, $\xi _{i,k}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$
 such that  \[p_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k}q_{i}+t\xi_{i,k}(t)q_{i})\in I.\]
 We denote
\[z_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k}q_{i}+t\xi_{i,k}(t)q_{i})   .\]
Hence \[p_{k}-z_{k}\in I.\]


 Let $r\in I.$ Then $r = \sum_{i=1}^{n'} s_{i}(t)p_i$ for some $s_i(t)\in \mathbb C \{t\}$ and some $n'$.  
Observe that $p_i-z_i\in I$, so
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n'} s_i(t) z_i = r - \sum_{i=1}^{n'} s_i(t) (z_i-p_{i})\in I.\]

Note that 
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n'} s_i(t)z_i\in \sum_{i=1}^n q_i \mathbb C\{t\} = \sum_{i=1}^n q_i\alpha_i\]
for some $\alpha_i\in \mathbb C\{t\}$.  It follows that $\sum_{i=1}^n q_i\alpha_i\in I$. Recall that by an earlier result from this proof it follows that $\alpha_i=0$.
Therefore,  $r - \sum_{i=1}^t s_i(t) (z_i-p_{i})=0$, as required.
   
\end{proof}


\begin{lemma}\label{pierwiastki} Let $l\in \mathbb R$. 
 Let notation be as in subsection \ref{333}, so $g_{k,l}(x)$ denotes the polynomial $g_{k}(x)$  specialised at $t=l$. Then for sufficiently small $l>0$, $g_{k,l}(x)$ is a polynomial of the same degree ($x$-degree) as $g_{k}(t)$, and it has no multiple roots.
\end{lemma} 
\begin{proof}
 Fix $i\leq n$. Let $g_{i}(t)=a_{0}(t)+a_{1}(t)x+\cdots + a_{m}(t)x^{m}$ for some polynomials
 $a_{0}(t), a_{1})(t), \ldots , a_{m}(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]$ where $ a_{m}(t)\neq 0$. By assumption $a_{m}(t)=1$, so $g_{i,s}(x)$ has the same degree as $g_{i}(x)$.  
 
 By the assumption $g_{i}(x)$ has no multiple roots so $g_{i}(x)$ and its derivative $g_{i}(x)'$ have no common roots.
Let ${\bar {\mathbb C}}[t]$ denote the field of fractions of  ${\mathbb C}[t]$.
 By the Bezout Lemma for polynomial rings over a field there are polynomials  $p(x), q(x)$ in variable $x$ and coefficients from $ {\bar {\mathbb C}}[t]$ and  such that 
$p(x)g_{i}(x)+q(x)g_{i}(x)'=1$.

Therefore, there are polynomals
$P(x)(t), Q(x)(t), r(x)(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t][x]$ such that $r(x)\neq 0$ and 
$P(x)g_{i}(x)+Q(x)g_{i}(x)'=r(x)$.
Specialising at $t=l$ for sufficiently small $l>0$ we have $r(x)(l)\neq 0$, hence  
we get  $P(x)(l)g_{i,l}(x)+Q(x)(l)g_{i,l}(x)'=1$ where $P(x)(l), Q(x)(l)\in {\mathbb C}[x]$.
 Therefore $g_{i,l}(x)$ and its derivative $g_{i,l}(x)'$ have no common roots, so $g_{i,l}(x)$ has no multiple roots. This concludes the proof. \end{proof}
  

Let notation be as in subsection \ref{333}.  Recall that $\sigma :{\mathbb C}\langle x,y\rangle  \rightarrow Im(\sigma) $ is a homomorphism of
 algebras, $\sigma (x)=f(x)(l)$, $\sigma (y)=f(y)(l)$, $\sigma (u_{i})=v_{i}$ and  
 $Im(\sigma )$ is a $\mathbb C$-algebra. 

\begin{lemma}\label{12} Let notation be as in Subsection \ref{333}.  We denote $f(x)=f(x)(t)$, $f(y)=f(y)(t)$, since they depend on $t$.   Suppose that 
 elements $f(x)(s)$ and $f(y)(s)$ generate $n$-dimensional ${\mathbb C}$-algebra for some $s$ and we can choose $s$ arbitrarily close to $0$. 
Then there is $e>0$ such that for each $l\neq 0$, $l\in [-e,e]$ elements $f(x)(l)$ and $f(y)(l)$ generate $Im(\sigma)$. Moreover, $Im(\sigma )$ is isomorphic to $\bar A$ . 
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}  Let $M(t), M'(t), u(t), v, e_{i}$ be as in Proposition \ref{basisnew}. Recall that $det(M(t))\neq 0$.  Observe that $det(M(t))$ is a strongly convergent power series, so for real $l$ sufficiently close to $0$ we have $det(M(l))\neq 0$, so we can take such $l$. 
 Recall that  that  $u(t)=vM(t)$ implies $det(M(t))v=u(t)M'(t)$.  Therefore, 
 specialising at $t=l$ (with $l\neq 0$, $l\in [-e,e]$ we can specialise as $M'(t)$ and $M(t)$ have entries from $t^{m'}{\mathbb C}[t]$ for some $m'\in \mathbb Z$) and we get that  $\sigma (e_{1}), \ldots ,\sigma(e_{n})$ can be obtained by linear combinations (over $\mathbb C$) of elements $f(m_{1})(l), \cdots , f(m_{n})(l)$. 
Consequently $\sigma (f(x))=f(x)(l)$ and $\sigma (f(y))=f(y)(l)$ generate $\sigma (A')= \oplus_{i=1}^{k'}M_{n_{i}}({\mathbb C}[({ v}_{i})])$. 
 In the proof of Proposition \ref{basisnew}, elements $e_{1}, \ldots , e_{n}$ were chosen in such a way that they span  $A'$ as a linear space over $\mathbb C$, therefore $\sigma (e_{1}), \ldots ,\sigma(e_{n})$ span $Im(\sigma )$ as a $\mathbb C$-linear space. 

 By Lemma \ref{pierwiastki}, we have that ${\mathbb C}[v_{i}]$ is isomorphic (as a $\mathbb C$-algebra) to $\oplus_{i=1}^{d_{i}} {\mathbb C}$ where $d_{i}$ is the degree of $g_{i,l}(x)$ (and, by the above, the degree of $g_{i}(x)$). 
 Therefore, $Im(\sigma )$ is isomorphic to $\bar A$. 
 
On the other hand, by the definition of  $f(x)(l)$ and $f(y)(l)$, the $\mathbb C$-algebra generated by $f(x)(l)$ and $f(y)(l)$ is contained by  $Im(\sigma )$.
 By the first part of the proof, this algebra contains $\sigma (e_{i})$ , therefore it is $n$ dimensional. Consequently the $\mathbb C$-algebra generated by $f(x)(l)$ and $f(y)(l)$ 
 equals $Im(\sigma )$, and by the above is isomorphic to $\bar A$, as required.
  \end{proof}

 
\begin{lemma}\label{3new} Let assumptions and notation be as in subsection \ref{333}.
 Let the notation and the assumptions be as in Proposition \ref{basesnew}. 
  Then there is a real number $\epsilon >0$ such that 
 for every $i,k$ the power series  $\xi _{i,k,}(t)$ is absolutely convergent at the  interval 
$(-\epsilon , \epsilon)$. Moreover $\xi _{i,k}(t)={\frac {h(t)}{g(t)}}$ for some polynomials $h(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]$, $g(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]$, moreover $g(t)\notin t{\mathbb C}[t]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof} By the proof of  Proposition \ref{basisnew} we obtain that 
 there are polynomials  $q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots , q_{n}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle [t]$ such that 
 the leading pseudoterms of $f(q_{1}), f(q_{2}), \ldots , f(q_{n})$
  are $e_{1}t^{j_{1}}, e_{2}t^{j_{2}}, \cdots , e_{n}t^{j^{n}}$, and $e_{1}, e_{2}, \ldots , e_{n}$ form a base of $A$, where $A$ is a linear space defined at the beginning of Subsection \ref{A}.    
  As in  Proposition \ref{basisnew}, this implies  that for any $g_{1}(t), \ldots , g_{n}(t)\in \mathbb C [t]$ (not all zero) we have \[g_{1}(t)f(q_{1})+
g_{2}(t)f(q_{2})+\ldots +g_{n}f(q_{n})\neq 0.\]
 (since its leading term is not zero).

 We can write $f(q_{j})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i}\alpha _{j,i}(t)$ for some $\alpha_{j,i}(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]t^{-\gamma }$, where $\gamma $ is as in subpoint $4$ in subsection \ref{333}.  
 Let $M$ be a square matrix of dimension $n$ whose $j$-th row (for each $j$) is 
\[  \alpha _{j,1}(t), \alpha _{j,2}(t), \ldots , \alpha _{j,n}(t).\]
 Then  $u^{T}=Mv^{T}$ where $u=[f(q_{1}), f(q_{2}), \ldots , f(q_{n})]^{T}$ and  
$v=[e_{1}, \ldots , e_{n}]$ and $v^{T}$ is the transpose of $v$.

$ $

Observe that $det(M)\neq 0$ by  the above property and that 
\[g_{1}(t)f(q_{1})+g_{2}(t)f(q_{2})+\ldots +g_{n}(t)f(q_{n})\neq 0.\]
 
 Therefore, by the proof of Lemma \ref{12} we have that $u^{T}=Mv^{T}$ implies $det(M) v^{T}=TMv^{T}=Tu^{T}$ where $u=[f(q_{1}), f(q_{2}), \ldots , f(q_{n})]^{T}$ and  
$v=[e_{1}, \ldots , e_{n}]$ and  $e_{1}, \ldots , e_{n}$ is a base of $A$.
Elements of $M$, $T$ are from $t^{-n\gamma }\mathbb C [t]$ (by the Cramer rules for the inverse of the matrix). 
 Let $det (M)=t^{\beta} h(t)$ for some number $\beta $ and some polynomial  $h(t)$ not divisible by $t$. Then, $h(t)=(t-\alpha _{1})\cdots (t-\alpha _{j})$ for some $\alpha _{1}, \ldots , \alpha _{j}\in \mathbb C$. Then, $h(t)^{-1}\in \mathbb C\{t\}$ is a strongly  convergent power series on some interval $(-e, e)$ with $0<e\in \mathbb R$. Therefore, $t^{\beta '}e_{i}=M'u^{T}$ where $M'=T\cdot h(t)^{-1}$ is an $n$ by $n$ matrix whose coefficients are absolutely convergent power series at some interval $(-e',e')$ and $\beta '=n\gamma +\beta $. 
 Therefore we have obtained the following fact:

{\em Fact 1.}  There is a natural number $\beta '$ such that  for each $j$ we have that $t^{\beta }e_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s _{i,j}(t)f(q_{i})$ where each $s_{i,j}(t)\in \mathbb C\{t\}$ 
 is an absolutely  convergent power series at the interval $(-e,e)$. Moreover, $s_{i,j}(t)={\frac {g_{i,j}(t)}{h(t)}}$, where $g_{i,j}(t), h(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]$, $h(t)\notin t {\mathbb C}[t]$. 

$ $

{\em Fact 2.} Observe now that by the point $3$ from Proposition \ref{basesnew}, $s _{i,k}(t)$ are unique.

$ $

 We will now finish the proof of our lemma. 
Let $j$ be a natural number, then if $p_{j}\in \{q_{1}, \ldots , q_{n}\}$  then the result holds
 (as then all $\xi_{i,k}=0$ except of just one $\xi_{i,k}=1$).
This happens, for example, when  $p_{1}=q_{1}=1$. 


 We know that  $f(p_{k})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i,k}(t)f(q_{i}),$ where $\gamma _{i,k}\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$. 

On the other hand, by the definition of $f$ we have
  $f(p_{k})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i,k}(t)e_{i}$,
 where $\gamma _{i,k}(t)\in t^{-\gamma}{\mathbb C}[t]$. 
 Therefore 
\[t^{\gamma +\beta }f(p_{k})\in \sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb C}[t]e_{i}t^{\beta }\subseteq h(t)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb C}[t]f(q_{i}),\] by Fact $1$, where  
 $ h(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]$, $h(t)\notin t {\mathbb C}[t]$.

 On the other hand, by the above  
\[f(p_{k})t^{\gamma +\beta}\in \sum_{i=1}^{n}f(q_{i}){\mathbb C}\{t\}t^{\gamma +\beta }.\] 
 By Fact $2$ we obtain  
$f(p_{k})t^{\gamma +\beta}\in \sum_{i=1}^{n}f(q_{i})h(t)^{-1}{\mathbb C}[t]t^{\gamma +\beta }.$
 Therefore
\[f(p_{k})\in \sum_{i=1}^{n}f(q_{i})h(t)^{-1}{\mathbb C}[t],\]
 as required. 

$ $

Observe $g(t)\notin t{\mathbb C}[t]$ since $\xi_{i,j}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$). 

\end{proof}


\begin{prop}\label{prop:relnew} Let notation and assumptions be as in subsection \ref{333}.
    Let $p_k$ be as in Notation \ref{not:monomials}. For any $k, m\in\{1,2,\dots, n\}$ there exist $\zeta _{i,k}\in \mathbb C$, $\xi _{i,k}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$ such that

\begin{proof} It follows from Lemma \ref{3new}.

\begin{notation}\label{bar q} Denote \[q_{i}=\bar {q}_{i}+{\tilde {q}}_{i},\]
 where $\bar {q}_{i}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle$ and $\tilde {q}_{i}\in t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$.
 Then  
\[ p_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k}\bar {q}_{i}\in I+t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}.\]

\begin{notation}\label{not:N} Let notation and assumptions be as in subsection \ref{333}.
We denote by $J$ the set consisting of $\mathbb C$-linear combinations of elements

    p_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k}\bar {q}_{i}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle,

where $\zeta _{i,k}$ are as in Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}.
 Let $\langle J\rangle $ be the ideal of $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle$ generated by elements from $J$. Further, let $N$ be the quotient algebra $ \mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle/\langle J\rangle$. 
 Notice that by Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}
\[{\bar {q}_{k}}{\bar {q}_{m}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k,m}{\bar {q}_{i}}\in \langle J\rangle .\]
 \end{notation}

 
\begin{lemma}\label{2new}
We have $e\in J$ if and only if  $e+e'\in I$ for some $e'\in t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$. In particular $J\subseteq I+t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$, and hence $\langle J\rangle \subseteq I+t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$.  
\end{lemma} 
\begin{proof} 
   The proof is the same  the proof of Lemma $3.4$ in \cite{DDS} (the only difference is that we use power series instead of polynomials). We repeat it for convenience of the reader: 
 If $e\in J$, then by Notation \ref{not:N}, $e = \sum_i \beta_i (p_k-l_k)$ where $l_k = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k}\bar {q}_{i} $ and $\beta_i\in \mathbb C$. Then let 
    \[{l'_k} = \sum_i \zeta_{ik}{\tilde {q_i}}+\sum_i t\xi_{ik}(t)q_i. \]
     Then $e'= \sum_i \beta_i {l'_i}$ is such that $e+e'\in I$ by Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}.

    Suppose on the other hand that $e\in \mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle$ is such that $e+e'\in I$ for some $e'\in \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$. Then by Proposition \ref{basisnew} we get that
    \[e+e' \in \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb C\{t\}(p_i-t_i),\]
    where $t_i=\sum_i (\zeta_{ik}q_i + t\xi_{ik}(t) q_i)$. So 
    $e+e' = \sum_i \alpha_i (p_i-t_i)$ 
    for some $\alpha_i\in \mathbb C\{t\}$. Let $\alpha_i = r_i+{\bar r}_i$ where $r_i\in \mathbb C$ and ${\bar r}_i\in \mathbb C\{t\}$. Denote $l_k = \sum_{i=1}^n \zeta_{ik}q_i$. By  
 comparing terms containing $t$ it follows that 
    \[e = \sum_i r_i(p_i-l_i).\]
    So $e\in J$, as required.

    Notice that if $e\in J$ then $e+e'\in I$, where $e'\in t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$ by a previous result of this proof. Therefore 
    \[e\in I-e' \in I+t\mathbb C \langle x,y \rangle \{t\}.\]
    Note that $e$ is an arbitrary element from $J$, so 
    $J\subseteq I+t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}$, hence 
    $\langle J\rangle\subseteq \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}+I.$

\end{proof}


\begin{prop}\label{3newest} The dimension of $N$ equals $n$. Moreover,  elements $\bar {q}_{k}+J\in N$ are a basis of $N$ as a $\mathbb C$-vector space.
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}  We use the same proof as the proof of Proposition $3.5$ in \cite{DDS}, but we  use power series instead of polynomials. Recall that by Proposition \ref{basisnew}
 \[\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle\subseteq \sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb C \{t\}{ {q}_{k}}+ I.\]
 
 
Recall that $q_{k}-{\bar q}_{k}\in t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle\{t\}$. 
Moreover, ${\bar q}_{k}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle$.  Notice also that $J\subseteq \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle $. It follows that

\[\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle\subseteq
 \sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb C {\bar {q}_{k}}+\langle J\rangle+t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle\{t\},\]
and hence  
$\{{\bar {q}_{k}}+\langle J\rangle\mid k\in \{1,2, \ldots ,n\}\}$  span $N$ as a $\mathbb C$-vector space.
 Therefore  the dimension of $N$ does not exceed $n$.

We now show that the elements ${\bar {q}_{k}}+\langle J\rangle\in N$ for $k\in \{1,2, \ldots ,n\}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$.
Suppose on the contrary that we have
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}{\bar {q}_{i}}\in \langle J\rangle \]
for some $\xi _{i}\in \mathbb {C}$. By Corollary \ref{2new} and Proposition \ref{basisnew} we have  \[\langle J\rangle \subseteq I+t\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}\subseteq I+t\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb C}\{t\}{ {q}_{i}}.\]
 Recall that \[q_{i}-\bar {q}_{i}\in t\mathbb C\langle x, y \rangle \{t\}\subseteq t(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb C \{t\}q_{i}+ I).\]
 Therefore \[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}{\bar {q}_{i}}\in \langle J\rangle \] implies
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}{ {q}_{i}}\in \langle J\rangle  + t(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb C\{t\}q_{i}+ I)\subseteq I+t\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb C}\{t\}{ {q}_{i}}. \]
 It follows that there is $e'\in t\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb C}\{t\}q_{i}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi _{i}q_{i}-e'\in I$, contradicting Proposition \ref{basisnew}. 
\end{proof}


 Observe now that the following holds.
\begin{prop}\label{7new} Let notation and assumptions be as in subsection \ref{333}. We can present $N$ as an $\mathbb C$-algebra 
 with generators $d_{1},\dots, d_n$ which span $N$ as a $\mathbb C$-vector space subject to relations 
\[ d_{k}d_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i},\] 
where $\zeta_{i,k,m}$ are as in Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}.

\end{prop}
\begin{proof}  We use the same  proof as in Proposition $3.6$ \cite{DDS} but we adjust it to the context of  power series.

We let ${\mathbb C}\langle{\bar {q}_{1}}, \ldots , {\bar {q}_{n}}\rangle$ be the  subalgebra of $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle$ generated by elements ${\bar {q}_{1}}, \ldots , {\bar {q}_{n}}\in \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle$. Similarly, let $\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle$ be the free $\mathbb C$-algebra generated by elements $d_{1}, \ldots , d_{n}$.  Let $\zeta:\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle\rightarrow \mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle/\langle J\rangle $ be defined as $\zeta (d_{i})={\bar {q}_{i}}+\langle J\rangle$.

We now show that $x+\langle J\rangle,y+\langle J\rangle\in  im(\zeta)$. Notice that since $f(x)\in im (f)$ we have
\[f(x)\in \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{\mathbb C}\{t\}f(q_i).\]
Hence we have $f(x)=f(x')$ for some $x'\in \sum_{i=0}^{n}{\mathbb C}\{t\}q_i. $ Then $x-x'\in I$, and so $x-x''\in  J$ for some $x''\in \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{\mathbb C}{\bar {q}_i}$. Indeed, if $x'=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(h_{i}+tg_{i}(t))q_{i}$ where $h_{i}\in \mathbb C$,  $g_{i}(t)\in \mathbb C\{t\}$ then $x''=\sum_{i=1}^{n} h_{i}{\bar q}_{i}$.  Then $x''+\langle J\rangle \in im (\zeta)$, and so $x+\langle J\rangle \in im (\zeta)$. An analogous argument shows $y+\langle J\rangle \in im (\zeta )$.

 Let \[J'=\ker (\zeta )\subseteq \mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle.\]
 Then by the First Isomorphism Theorem for rings $\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle/J'$ is isomorphic to 
$ im (\zeta )=\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle/\langle J\rangle =N$. 

Let $J''$ be the ideal of $\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle$ generated by  elements 
\[ d_{k}d_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i}\]
where $\zeta_{i,k,m}$ are as in Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}. Observe that 
\[\zeta \left (d_{k}d_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i} \right)={\bar {q}_{k}}{\bar {q}_{m}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k,m}{\bar {q}_{i}}+\langle J\rangle =0+\langle J\rangle .\] 
 Therefore $J''\subseteq J'$. It follows that  the dimension of $ \mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle/J'$ does not exceed the dimension of $ \mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle/J''$. 
 
 We now show that $J'=J''$. Notice that $\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle/J''$ is at most $n$-dimensional since every element can be presented as a linear combination of elements $d_{i}+J''$ for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. On the other hand 
$\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle/J'$ is isomorphic to 
 $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle/\langle J \rangle $, and hence is $n$-dimensional (by Proposition \ref{3newest}). Hence by comparing dimensions we get  that $J'=J''$, as required.

\end{proof}

We now define a multiplication on $N$ which gives a formal deformation to the algebra $A$. 


\begin{theorem} \label{thm formal deformationnew}
Let $d_1,\dots,d_n$ be free generators of the $\mathbb C$-algebra $\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle$ and suppose $\zeta _{i,k,m}\in \mathbb C$, $\xi _{i,k,m}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$ are as in Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}. Then the multiplication rule
\[d_{k} \ast_t d_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i}+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)d_{i}).\]
 gives a formal deformation such that $\ast_0$ gives the multiplication on $N$. 
 
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof} 
     We use an analogous proof as in Theorem $3.7$ \cite{DDS} but we adjust it to the context of power series (instead of polynomials) and add some additional explanations. 
 Recall relations from Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}, that for any $k, m\in\{1,2,\dots, n\}$  there exist $\zeta _{i,k,m}\in \mathbb C$, $\xi _{i,k,m}(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relI}
    q_{k}q_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}q_{i}+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)q_{i})\in I.
\end{equation}
 
We introduce the notation $[q_{i}]:=q_{i}+I$ for elements of $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle\{t\}/I$. Hence we obtain the following relations corresponding to (\ref{eq:relI}) which give the  multiplicative table  on $\mathbb C\langle x,y \rangle \{t\}/I$. We have
\[[q_{k}] [q_{m}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}[q_{i}]+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)[q_{i}])=[0].\]
 
Notice that these relations give a multiplication
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def0}
  d_{k} \ast_t d_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i}+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)d_{i})  
\end{equation}
for $d_i\in \mathbb C\langle d_{1}, \ldots , d_{n} \rangle.$ Now recall that by Proposition \ref{7new} $N$ is 
 given by generators ${d}_{1}, \ldots , d_{n}$ subject to relations   
 $d_{k}d_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i}.$
  Therefore $*_{0}$ is the multiplication on $N$.

{\em Remark.} Fix natural numbers $i',j',k'$. To see that  the multiplicative table is well defined (so that these relations give a  Groebner Bases) observe that by using 
 the formulas \[[q_{k}] [q_{m}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}[q_{i}]+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)[q_{i}])\]
  for various $k,m$ several times (and without using any other formulas) we obtain
 
$([q_{i'}][q_{j'}])[q_{k'}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{l}(t)[q_{l}]$
and 
\[[q_{i'}]([q_{j'}][q_{k'}])=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{l}'(t)[q_{l}],\] for some $d_{l}(t), d_{l}'(t)\in {\mathbb C}\{t\}$.

Because of the associativity we get
 $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(d_{l}(t)-d_{l}'(t))[q_{l}]=0$
  and hence 
 $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(d_{l}(t)-d_{l}'(t))[q_{l}]\in I$, and by Proposition \ref{basesnew}
we get $d_{l}(t)=d_{l}'(t)$.

Now this implies that $d_{i'}(d_{j'}d_{k'})=d_{i'}(d_{j'}d_{k'})$. This is because we can use the same steps when using relations  \[d_{k} d_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}d_{i}+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)d_{i})\] instead of relations \[[q_{k}] [q_{m}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\zeta _{i,k,m}[q_{i}]+t\xi_{i,k,m}(t)[q_{i}])\].

\end{proof}

By the assumption elements $f(x)(s)$ and

\subsection{ Deformations of polynomial type}

We will now show that our third method produces deformations of polynomial type. The same proof can be used to  show that the second method gives deformations of polynomial type.

 Let $\zeta _{i,j,k}, \xi _{i,j,k}$ be as in Proposition \ref{prop:relnew}. We know that  $\zeta _{i,j,k}+t\xi_{i,j,k}(t)$ are rational functions in variable $t$ and so there are  $\sigma _{i,j,k}(t), h(t)\in {\mathbb C}[t]$ such that for all $1\leq i,j,k\leq n$  such that \[\zeta _{i,j,k}+\xi_{i,j,k}(t)= h(t)^{-1}\sigma_{i,j,k}(t).\]
We can assume that $h(t)=1+{\bar h}(t)$, where ${\bar h}(t)\in t{\mathbb C}[t]$ (since we can adjust $\sigma _{i,j,k}$). 

  The main result in this section is: 
\begin{theorem}\label{polynomial}   
Let notation and assumptions be as in subsection \ref{333} and as at the begining of this subsection.
Let $d_1,\dots,d_n$ be free generators of the $\mathbb C$-algebra $\mathbb C\langle d_1,\dots, d_n \rangle$. Then the multiplication rule
\[d_{k} \circ _t d_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma _{i,k,m}(t)d_{i}\]
 gives a formal deformation such that $\circ _0$ gives the multiplication on a $\mathbb C$- algebra (generated by $d_{1}, \ldots , d_{n}$) isomorphic to $N$.  
Moreover, for all $l>0$ sufficiently close to $0$, the multiplication $\circ _{l}$ gives the multiplication on the $\mathbb C$-algebra (generated by $d_{1}, \ldots , d_{n}$) isomorphic to $\bar A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof} We know that  $\zeta _{i,j,k}+t\xi_{i,j,k}(t)= h(t)^{-1}\sigma_{i,j,k}(t)$ and $h(t)=1+{\bar h}(t)$ where ${\bar h}(t)\in t{\mathbb C}[t]$. 
 Then $\sigma _{i,j,k}(t)=(1+{\bar h}(t))(\zeta _{i,j,k}+t\xi_{i,j,k}(t))\in  \zeta _{i,j,k}+ t{\mathbb C}[t]$.
 Therefore, at $t=0$ we have
 \[d_{k} \ast_{0} d_{m}=d_{k} \circ _{0} d_{m},\] 
 where $\ast _{t}$ is as in Theorem  \ref{thm formal deformationnew}.
 Consequently, by Theorem \ref{thm formal deformationnew}  the multiplication rule 
\[d_{k} \ast_t d_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma _{i,j,k}(t)d_{i}).\]
 gives a formal deformation ${\mathcal N}'$ of $N$.

$ $ 

{\bf Fact $1$.}  We now consider specialisation ${\mathcal N}$ at $t=s$. 
 Let $\ast _{t}$ and  $s>0$ be as in Theorem \ref{thm:iso1new} so that the multiplication $\ast _{s}$ gives an algebra (generated by $d_{1}, \ldots , d_{n}$ isomorphic to $\bar A$) for sufficiently small $s>0$.
By Lemma \ref{12}  we can take $s$ arbitrarily close to $0$, so 
 we can take $s$ such that $h(s)\neq 0$. 
  %Denote $a_{i}=h(t)d_{i}$ for $i=1,\ldots , n$. 
  This gives  
$(d_{k}h(t))\ast _{t}(d_{m}h(t))= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma _{i,j,k}(t)(d_{i}h(t))$.

 $ $

 When specialising at $t=s$ we have 
$(d_{k}h(s))\ast _{s}(d_{m}h(s))= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma _{i,j,k}(s)(d_{i}h(s))$.

  The $\mathbb C$ algebra generated by elements 
 $d_{1}h(s), \ldots , d_{n}h(s)$ generate  an algebra (which we call $N'$) with multiplication $\ast _{s}$  is a subalgebra  of the  algebra (which we call $N''$) generated by $d_{1}, \ldots , d_{n}$ and multiplication $\ast _{s}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:iso1new}, $N''$ is isomorphic to $\bar A$.
 Observe that  $N''\subseteq N'$ since $d_{i}=h(s)^{-1}(d_{i}h(s))\in N'$, so $N'=N''$. So $N'$ is ismorphic to $\bar A$. 

$ $

 Consider now specialisation $N_{s}'$ of algebra ${\mathcal N}'$ at $t=s$.
 Denote $d_{k}=a_{k}$. Then $N'$ has generators $a_{1}, \ldots , a_{n}$, and is defined by relations:
 $a_{k}\circ _{s}a_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma _{i,j,k}(t)a_{i}$.

 This algebra can be homomorphically mapped onto algebra $N'$ when we map $a_{i}\rightarrow d_{i}h(s)$ (since the images of all generating relations of $N'$ are zero in $N_{s}'$). Consequently  $N_{s}'$ can be homomorphically mapped  onto $N'$ and hence  onto ${\bar A}$. Observe that $N_{s}'$ is spanned by elements $a_{1}, \ldots , a_{n}$ so has dimension at most $n$. On the other hand, ${\bar A}$  has dimension $n$. Consequently, $N_{s}'$ is isomorphic to ${\bar A}$.  
  

\end{proof}
